a1.section: 1 · The broken spec — what actually wins
a1.question: The spec doc's stack (Next.js / Vercel / Supabase / RLS / pgvector) conflicts with the Brimba-on-Cloudflare base. Which wins?
a1.selected: Cloudflare + Brimba wins everywhere - treat the doc's stack sections as void, keep its product and data rules

a2.section: 1 · The broken spec — what actually wins
a2.question: Concretely: the doc leans on Postgres RLS policies (auth_person_id, auth_customer_ids helpers). Brimba's model is physical isolation - each tenant gets its OWN D1 database, so a portal session can only ever touch its own data, plus a permission matrix (role_permissions) for what members can do inside it. Accept that as the security model, replacing RLS?
a2.selected: Yes - per-tenant D1 isolation + the base's role permission matrix replaces RLS

a3.section: 1 · The broken spec — what actually wins
a3.question: The doc requires the database in the EU region for GDPR. On Cloudflare: D1 supports location hints, R2 supports EU jurisdiction, but Workers execute globally. How strict is the residency requirement really?
a3.notes: Let's ensure that literally everything that we can do via Cloudflare is on European servers, if possible. I know there will be some limitations if we externally use APIs or call APIs to AI models. That's fine, but other than that, everything is on EU servers.

a4.section: 1 · The broken spec — what actually wins
a4.question: The doc demands background task queues (sagas) for every third-party call: Drive exports, Resend notifications, Calendar syncs - so an offline external API never breaks a DB transaction. Brimba has NO queue infrastructure today (one nightly cron + Durable Objects for realtime). What carries the sagas?
a4.notes: I don't know what sagas are, but I would just assume that these are scheduled workflows, right? I don't know, man. You decide what is best, whatever you can find in Cloudflare infrastructure that can support this at scale with robust quality and allow us a lot of analysis and visibility into logs and something that we can document very well. Let's just use that.

a5.section: 1 · The broken spec — what actually wins
a5.question: The doc's build order is Blocks 0-7 (Foundations, Contacts, Business Map, Delivery, Tickets+Sagas, Drive+RAG, Surfaces, Commercial+Calendar). Brimba already provides most of Blocks 0-1 (monorepo, auth, tenancy, roles, permission matrix). Does the ordering still hold?
a5.notes:
I want to revisit the meaning of:
- foundations
- business map
- deliveries
- sagas
- surfaces
- commercial calendar
What the hell are all these terms? I think we need to get our terminology straight here.

c1.section: 3 · Tenancy, contacts and the customer switcher
c1.question: Does customer = tenant? I.e., each Kwapso customer company gets its own isolated tenant database holding their apps, processes, steps, tickets and file index?
c1.notes: There is no need for this because we will just be operating under one team, which is the Kwapso team. The whole concept of multi-tenancy and every time there is a new tenant, we spin up a new database, still exists, but this time there will always and only be one tenant. The only thing that we need to keep in mind is that if this particular one tenant's databases start to grow beyond expectation, we just have to dip into our sharding mechanism that we already built.

c2.section: 3 · Tenancy, contacts and the customer switcher
c2.question: The spec's unified contacts table wants every person - staff, client logins, and non-login participants (field workers who appear in process steps but never sign in) - in ONE place. Brimba already keeps login users global with per-team memberships. Where do the non-login people live?
c2.notes: I don't understand what this means. The contacts table is a place where we literally store all of our clients as either entities and their points of contact. There is a users table that is designed to authenticate which users from our internal team can log in and which clients can log in. Of course, we can leverage that data to then set permission matrices and other things and member rules, etc.

c3.section: 3 · Tenancy, contacts and the customer switcher
c3.question: Concretely: Maria is CFO of two companies you serve. She logs in once and flips between them with the header switcher (Brimba's team switcher already does this). When she creates a ticket for customer A, which database wrote what?
c3.notes:
Look, man, I know that this is a static form, but I've told you that we are the only tenant. Therefore, there is no multi-tenancy, technically, and the ability to create new teams or hop teams and all of that is technically disabled.

If there is Maria, who's a CFO of two companies we are building for, Maria just logs into the client portal with her email. Because she is a stakeholder of one or more apps, she'll be able to enter both those apps and see the relevant details in their details screens, etc.

She can log in because her name is in the users table, yes, somebody's name and company details, or a company entity or a private individual as a contact person of an entity. All of that can remain in the contacts table. Unless and until somebody goes into the contact and adds as a user who is not added to the users table (they are not part of our team member in the client portal or a client portal member or a user), they cannot log in, even if they exist in the contacts table.

c4.section: 3 · Tenancy, contacts and the customer switcher
c4.question: Agency-side data - sprints, stories, work logs, rate cards, margins - is commercially sensitive and spans all customers. Where does it live?
c4.notes:
Sprints are their own database, one per tenant, and since we only have one tenant, one database. Keep in mind I've said it before: sharding laws apply, right? This should scale even if our database was to get full. That means we open up a new database and whatever we've designed in Brimba to work at large-scale sharding and joining on serving data across multiple databases per tenant, and making sure that MCPs, APIs, and all of that work perfectly.

I'm saying sprints are separate database stories, separate database work logs, of course, separate database. Let's even throw in an activity table every time somebody creates, edits, or archives any sort of record. An activity is recorded, and I know this is commercially sensitive and spans all customers. I don't know where it should live, but we should have some kind of secure functionality to only serve this data to one if the customer has the correct access rights to view it and the data belongs to any of their apps. It will all be determined as to how we set up roles and stakeholders.

c5.selected: Live is required - design for fan-out queries

- processes have their own permission matrix
- steps, etc.
If we have to merge something to put it into a module-level umbrella, I will let you know.

d4.question: Impersonation mode (staff viewing the portal as a client) must be read-only and logged with both identities. Where is read-only enforced?
d4.notes: Well, this is a good point. I don't know how exactly this can be done. Are you suggesting we create some sort of back door? I don't like the idea of that. I want something to be truly private and truly secure, but what we could do to test it out whenever we do get to a point where we can preview and test these things out and provide feedback is that we could just create a fake contact with fake contact people, right?

d5.question: The onboarding gate: first portal login is blocked until the main stakeholder confirms the team map + company metadata (headcount, founding year). Is this v1, and what happens if they stall for weeks?
d5.selected: V1, soft gate - persistent banner but the portal works

e1.question: One active timer per person globally. A person starts timer B while timer A is running. What happens?
e1.notes:
I don't understand what this means. If there are multiple people working on multiple things, or even the same thing, it shouldn't matter because the work log creates a brand-new start and stop row per user per story per task or whatever. Given that we have a work log that is an append-only table, it doesn't matter if there is one active timer per person globally or anything like that. They're all just rows getting added and appended.  
  
When we want to know the breakdown, we can simply analyse all those work log rows per story, per session, per sprint, or whatever, because the work log is the most indivisible unit of how time at work is spent by each and every person. Therefore, it will contain all nested-level data, like whether it's part of a task or a story or a sprint, etc.

e2.question: Timer stop lands on integer minutes how?
e2.notes: Keep the timer accurate. If it's 33 seconds, then it's 33 seconds. If it's 192 seconds, round up to the nearest second.

e3.question: A timer left running overnight - 14 hours by mistake. What does the system do?
e3.notes: Any work log that has taken... I am not sure, because sometimes things just take two days. That doesn't mean I've stayed up all night to finish it, but it just seems like an unnecessary task to do: to start and stop each and everything that I'm working on that spans 1 or 2 days, or 3 or 4 days, to turn it on and off every night and morning. Do you recommend something?

e4.question: Work logs carry the commercial engagement type (blueprint, sprint, support, hourly). Who sets it?
e4.selected: Inherited and locked - only admins reclassify
e4.notes: All this data can be inherited. It can also be edited. It can also be picked from a required drop-down. Most likely, it is not locked, but if somebody has the ability to edit work logs equal to true from the permission matrix, then they can edit it.

e5.question: Peer review before story close: reviewer must be the App's lead and cannot be the assignee. In a 2-3 person team the lead often IS the assignee. What then?
e5.notes: I think this is fine, right, if it's a small team and the reviewer is also the assignee, even though it's unlikely to happen for us because now we're a dev team of four people. Even if it does, if the reviewer is the assignee, then it's very simple: the rule applies because I am also a reviewer. I can review my own task because this is not a systemic rule failure. It is a failure on whoever tried to create or assign this task.

h3.section: 8 · Design language and the two surfaces
h3.question: Density tension: the spec demands dense, spreadsheet-style, keyboard-driven grids for the agency app; the brand is airy 24px-radius paper. Resolution?
h3.selected: Brand rules apply 100% to both surfaces, even datagrids
h3.notes: And ensure that, even in both places, the design language still is retained. I never want the client in the client portal or the internal staff member in the agency to ever feel cognitive load. It should be a delight to use these apps, so we have to be very good with the UI, the animations. It should be warm, exciting, inviting, and lazy cognitive displays. Essentially, don't show extra information. Only show the tip or summary of something through tabs, buttons, or components, and then, only when clicked or interacted with, we can show them more details. But please remember that we still need to leverage our existing UI library to do so. It is just how we arrange the sequence and use the UI library to build different screens that matters. We don't recreate components.
